primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- the February 1, 1994 letter Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban wrote to PCAGC Chairman Eufemio C. Domingo, putting in writing the constitutional and legal questions he raised about his appointment as the part-time Commissioner representing the private sector.

The tension he identifies between Executive Order No. 151-A, which contemplates a private-sector Commissioner serving part-time, and Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution together with Section 7(b)(2) of Republic Act 6713, which bar the private practice of a profession and participation in business.

His two precise questions: whether a part-time Commissioner may practice his profession and hold business positions while serving, and whether he is subject to the Statements and Disclosure provisions of RA 6713.

His insistence that the PCAGC, as the body created to set the example of following the anti-graft laws, should have these questions settled by a definitive ruling such as an Opinion of the Secretary of Justice before he takes his oath.
sub_topics: The occasion, per the editor's note: President Fidel V. Ramos appointed him on January 21, 1994 as the private-sector member of the Presidential Commission Against Graft and Corruption, with EO 151-A allowing part-time service.

The text of EO No. 151-A, Section 2, quoted: a Chairman and two Commissioners, one of whom shall represent the private sector and may serve on a part-time basis, with the ranks, emoluments and privileges of Presidential Assistants II and I.

The countervailing text of Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution, quoted: the President, Vice-President, Members of the Cabinet and their deputies or assistants shall not hold other office, practice any other profession, participate in any business or be financially interested in government contracts, and shall strictly avoid conflict of interest.

The penal reinforcement in Republic Act 6713, Section 7(b)(2), which bars public officials and employees from engaging in the private practice of their profession unless authorized and where it would conflict with official functions.

His reading of the EO's purpose: people empowerment through a Commissioner who remains in the private sector, since the office would be meaningless if the appointee could not continue his private work -- a policy under which many others have been appointed part-time and allowed to practice.

The threshold questions of coverage: whether the Chairman and Members of the Commission fall within 'Members of the Cabinet, their deputies and assistants,' and whether a part-time Commissioner is a 'public official' as defined in RA 6713.

The distinguishing of Civil Liberties Union versus The Executive Secretary (194 SCRA 317, 1991), where the Supreme Court's August 1, 1991 resolution confined the prohibition to heads of executive departments, undersecretaries and assistant secretaries -- but which involved holding other office, not private practice, and did not rule on part-time office under the Ethical Standards Law.

His two formal questions, the first naming his own stake: his senior partnership in Panganiban Benitez Parlade Africa and Barinaga and his directorships in Baron Travel Corporation and the Philippine Daily Inquirer, Inc.

His reason for asking before taking his oath: so that the Commission's acts and his own are not subject to attack or doubt, and because actions done in good faith under such an opinion would not incur sanctions under Section 10(b) of RA 6713.

stances.claim: The evident objective of Executive Order No. 151-A is people empowerment through a Commissioner who remains in the private sector, which presupposes that he may continue practising his profession or running his business -- for otherwise he could not represent the private sector at all.
stances.rhetorical_move: purposive reading of the EO, reinforced by a rhetorical question and by the existing practice of many part-time appointees

stances.claim: Civil Liberties Union versus The Executive Secretary does not settle his case, because its issue was the holding of another office rather than the private practice of a profession or participation in business, and the Court did not rule on the legality of a part-time office under the Ethical Standards Law.
stances.rhetorical_move: distinguishing the precedent by isolating its actual issue from the question presented

stances.claim: The questions must be put at rest by a definitive ruling such as an Opinion of the Secretary of Justice before he takes his oath, because the PCAGC is the executive entity created to set the example of faithfully following the anti-graft laws and its acts should not be open to attack or doubt.
stances.rhetorical_move: exemplarity argument: the anti-graft body held to a higher standard than the common practice it could have relied upon, with good-faith reliance under Section 10(b) as the practical safeguard

notable_anecdotes: He puts his own stake on the record, naming his senior partnership in Panganiban Benitez Parlade Africa and Barinaga and his directorships in Baron Travel Corporation and the Philippine Daily Inquirer, Inc. as the very interests the answer would decide.

He acknowledges that many other private individuals have already assumed part-time commissionerships and continued in their professions or businesses, yet declines to rest on that practice for himself.

The editor's note records the outcome: Opinion No. 33, Series of 1994 ruled that a part-time commissioner is subject to the same disabilities, disallowances and disqualifications as full-time commissioners, and rather than discontinue his private law practice he respectfully declined the post.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints the letter Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban addressed on February 1, 1994 to Hon. Eufemio C. Domingo, Chairman of the Presidential Commission Against Graft and Corruption, placing in writing the constitutional and legal questions he had raised about his appointment, made by President Fidel V. Ramos on January 21, 1994, as the Commissioner representing the private sector. He quotes Section 2 of Executive Order No. 151-A, which provides that one of the two Commissioners shall represent the private sector and may serve on a part-time basis, and sets against it Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution, which forbids the President, Vice-President, Members of the Cabinet and their deputies or assistants to hold other office, to practice any other profession, to participate in any business or to be financially interested in government contracts, as well as Section 7(b)(2) of Republic Act 6713, the Ethical Standards Law, which repeats the bar on private practice with penal sanctions and reaches all public officials and employees. Reading the executive order purposively, he argues that its objective is people empowerment through a Commissioner who remains in the private sector, since the office would be meaningless if the appointee could not continue his private work, and notes that many others have been appointed part-time on that understanding. He then poses the threshold questions of coverage and distinguishes Civil Liberties Union versus The Executive Secretary, 194 SCRA 317, whose August 1, 1991 resolution confined the prohibition to department heads, undersecretaries and assistant secretaries but concerned the holding of another office rather than private practice and did not pass on part-time office under the Ethical Standards Law. His two formal questions ask whether he may continue as senior partner of Panganiban Benitez Parlade Africa and Barinaga and as an officer and director of Baron Travel Corporation and the Philippine Daily Inquirer, Inc., and whether he is subject to the Statements and Disclosure provisions. He asks that the matter be settled by a definitive ruling, such as an Opinion of the Secretary of Justice, before he takes his oath, since the PCAGC of all bodies should set the example of following the anti-graft laws and its acts and his own should not be open to attack or doubt.
